messages.author: e6c87266ffc5f0f2
messages.subject: A plea for filling patterns
parts:
Hi,

I love ggplot and and many papers have figures generated by ggplot
in them However, I receive repeatedly push back from the reviewers and
also the copy editors that the colour figures don't work well with
black&white printing.

- I know that the problem doesn't reside with ggplot itself.
- I understand that the source code is open and I could in theory add
it myself.
- I understand that ggplot is free and I have to take it as is it.

Still—please register another vote in support of 'filling patterns'.

Are there any plans for it? Is there any light work (beta testing)
where one can help?

Thanks.

Many suggestions in the forums are either incomplete (not for general
polygons) or impractical. So let me add two more: (1) export from R to
tikz and then manually replace the colours with patterns, (2) export
from R and use gnuplot for figures where it matters. I want to go
neither of the two routes.

patterns anyway.

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Re: A plea for filling patterns
parts:
On Sat, Apr 9, 2011 at 00:42, Kasi <pop...@gmx.net> wrote:
> Many suggestions in the forums are either incomplete (not for general
> polygons) or impractical. So let me add two more: (1) export from R to
> tikz and then manually replace the colours with patterns,

I understand this will seem like an impractical solution too but at
least it is an easy enough workaround:
- use a colour scale
- export the plot to PDF or SVG
- open and modify it in Inkscape
- export PDF or EPS or whatever the publisher wants (they will
probably stupidly ask for 600dpi TIFFs) from Inkscape

Inkscape comes with functionality that will make the modifications easy"ish".

Selecting elements of the same colour
- select one element of a given colour
- right click on the colour swatch at the bottom left of the window
- select "Copy colour"
- Edit > Find (Ctrl+F)
- in the "Style" section, paste the colour (Ctrl+V)
- click "Find" or press "Enter"
This will select all elements with this colour in the plot. You can
edit them all at once (change their colour, fill them with a pattern,
etc.). To "save" this selection, just group the elements (Edit >
Group, Ctrl+G). You can later select the group and apply a certain
style to it.

Applying and modifying a pattern
- select an element
- in the fill and stroke panel, select a pattern
- select the node tool (second from top)
- handles appear at the top left of the page, they modify the pattern
- the square handle modify the size of the pattern, the round one
modifies the rotation

Applying the same style to several elements
- select the element with the style you want
- Edit > Copy (Ctrl+C)
- select all other elements you want the style applied to
- Edit > Paste style (Ctrl+Shift+V)
You can select one element inside a group by Ctrl+clicking on it,
modify it, copy it, then click elsewhere to clear the selection, click
on the group and paste style. The whole group will get the new style
you just defined.

Creating a pattern
- draw something on the canvas
- when this something has several elements, group them
- select the just created object/group and Object > Pattern > Object
to pattern (Alt+I)
- select an object you want to apply the pattern to
- in the Fill and Stroke dialog, select the new pattern in the pattern
list. It should be named something like "pattern12345"
The pattern will be repeated based on the bounding box of the original
object. So, as a rule of thumb, when designing a pattern, try to have
it fit in a rectangle. You will be able to modify its size and
orientation with the node tool after the pattern is applied anyway.

This might all seem complex but really, once you get the hang of how
Inkscape works, handles objects etc. it is very easy and quite fast.
Inkscape is remarkably consistent so, even if it is a powerful piece
of software, it should be easy to learn.


Reproducible research principles say you shouldn't do this. Practical
requirements show that, for me at least, it is much faster to get
decent enough plots from ggplot, choose among them and then polish the
few that will make it in the paper in Inkscape, even if I have to redo
the polishing once or twice because I redid the plot. There are things
like changing fonts, highlighting a part of a plot, rearranging the
legend, modify the spacing between plot elements that are only
reasonably done in an external software.

That's my two cents.

JiHO
